candidateReports.source: John Weidner, Very Good Ventures (passed Foundations, 738/1000)
candidateReports.summary: Passed on 30 May 2026 (online proctored) with 738 against a 720 cut, which is 44 of 60 correct; 'one more wrong answer would have put me under'. He prepared for 10 days with nightly Claude tutoring based on the exam guide and scored about 850 and 930 on practice runs. 'Nothing looked familiar' on the real exam, because the practice pool reuses questions and he had memorized answers rather than ideas. Domain scores: Agentic 78%, Context/Reliability 73%, Tool/MCP 70%, Claude Code config 69% (his weakest). Results took about 7 days.
tips: A high practice score is not readiness. Practice pools repeat questions, so learn the reasoning, not the answer key.
Build your own study tools and drills instead of relying only on screenshots of mock questions.
Budget under 2 minutes per question. Flag and move on when stuck.
Don't mistake AI encouragement for readiness. Test yourself on new scenarios.
For online proctoring, disconnect extra monitors (the software uses your camera and mic).

candidateReports.summary: Two weeks of prep at 90–120 minutes a night, in four phases: core architecture, hands-on Claude Code and MCP, context management, then timed mocks. They expected to memorize docs but got architectural judgment questions where several options were viable under cost, latency and reliability constraints. Most tested: agentic loops and stop_reason, tool orchestration, context management, CLAUDE.md, permissions and plan mode, MCP, structured output with JSON Schema, and agent failure modes.
tips: Ask 'What's the constraint?' before you read the options.
Biggest trap: assuming the more complex architecture is better. The exam rewards the simplest design that meets the requirements.
Write a one-page summary of each domain in your own words.
Finish with timed practice so the pacing feels normal.

candidateReports.summary: Took the exam at a test center on 24 Aug 2026 after more than a month of focused prep on top of daily Claude Code use since mid-2025. Mock scores went 766 → 846 → 901 → 903 → 915. He names three principles: enforcement over guidance, tool descriptions as the primary interface, and catching errors downstream with validators. He also names three common disguises for wrong answers: add more examples or description, switch to a stronger model, or ask the model to check itself. He started at 4–5 minutes per question, got under 2, and finished with 15 minutes to spare.
tips: 'If you need certainty, don't rely on a prompt.' Hooks, gates and validators beat instructions.
When a stem says 'a team member proposes X', X is almost always wrong.
Details that look redundant in a long scenario are qualifiers that rule out options.
Readiness gates: external mocks stably above 900, and you can explain every wrong answer.
Get hands-on first, and practice reading long English scenarios quickly.
Bring government photo ID that matches your registration (Latin script). Phone, watch and notes go in the locker.

candidateReports.source: Sofia Lemons, Udacity / Accenture LearnVantage (passed Foundations)
candidateReports.summary: Six weeks of prep on top of prior experience; she estimates a few months if you're new. She finished in about 90 of the 120 minutes, online proctored with webcam and screen share, and got results in 1–2 weeks. Two cross-cutting ideas: treat context as a budget (what does each agent actually need?) and match the strength of a guarantee to the business risk. Her weak areas were team Claude Code repos, CI/CD and large-scale testing.
tips: 'Several answer options will be plausible. Some will be functional in certain situations.' Pick the best fit for the stated constraint.
Watch for the 'pile on more few-shot examples' distractor when a better tool description is the cleaner fix.
Take the sample exam early and build small projects sooner.
Make prompt caching and batch processing concrete by calling the API yourself and watching the cost.

candidateReports.summary: Waited until she scored 900/1000 on the official practice exam before booking. The real questions used longer, more complex sentences with buried qualifiers, and git and CI/CD pipeline commands came up more than mocks suggested. She studied the exam guide, the FAQ, four Skilljar courses (Building with the Claude API, Claude Code in Action, Intro to Agent Skills, Intro to MCP), community GitHub guides and the claude-cookbooks.
tips: Slow down enough to find the qualifier in each long sentence before you choose.
Learn claude -p, --output-format json, --json-schema and the GitHub Action. CI/CD shows up more than mocks suggest.
Do the hands-on exercises in the exam guide instead of only reading.
Online exam: install the proctoring software early, use one screen, run no other AI tools, translators, IDEs or tabs, and keep the session open until the recording finishes uploading.

candidateReports.source: Test Engineering Notes (passed Developer CCDV-F and Architect CCAR-F)
candidateReports.summary: Spent 20–30 hours on hands-on work and mocks beyond the Partner Academy courses, using NotebookLM for quizzes and flashcards plus Udemy mocks. 'The main theme of the exam is trade-offs.' Some questions need general engineering knowledge (SDLC, non-functional requirements). Python SDK experience with sync, async and batch calls helps.
tips: Log in 30 minutes early. Pearson check-in takes time.
Strike out the obviously wrong options first.
Answer everything in one pass, then use the Review screen for flagged items.

candidateReports.source: Matthew Purcell (AWS), Professional 925/1000, relayed by findskill.ai (secondary source)
candidateReports.summary: Reported as the first publicly visible CCAR-P holder, scoring 925/1000, and has passed all four Claude exams. He says the Professional exam was 'noticeably less about API mechanics than the Foundations exam and much more about judgement', and easier than Foundations for an experienced practitioner. This is a secondary relay of a LinkedIn post that could not be read directly, so treat the details as anecdotal.
tips: Prepare for judgment and trade-off questions, not recall of API mechanics.
Real architecture experience counts for more than memorizing docs on this exam.

candidateReports.source: Szymon Paluch (passed Foundations; Professional prep write-up)
candidateReports.summary: A prep write-up for CCAR-P by an author who passed Foundations and works from the official Professional guide. He describes the Professional exam as 'enterprise deployment over pure coding', with scenario-style stems. His example: a healthcare client needs clinician review before replies go to patients, and the defensible answer is 'The requirement is a hard gate, so it belongs in the workflow, not in the prompt.' That example is his own illustration and is not in the official guide.
tips: Hard requirements such as mandatory human review belong in the workflow as gates, not in prompt instructions.
Expect enterprise deployment concerns: governance, security reviews, stakeholders.

candidateReports.source: avidevelops/claude-architect-exam-prep (community notes from a Q&A thread)
candidateReports.summary: Community-compiled notes from candidates who discussed the exam. One contributor called it 'a tricky paper… several options could technically solve the problem.' Principles they collected: enforce rules in the schema or backend rather than the prompt, use explicit IDs rather than matching on text, don't spawn a subagent if the coordinator already holds the context, and treat MCP annotations as untrusted.
tips: Enforce in the schema or backend, not in the prompt.
Pass explicit IDs (customer_id, order_id) instead of matching names or free text.
Don't spawn a subagent when the coordinator already has the context it needs.
Treat tool annotations from MCP servers as untrusted metadata.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Name the constraint before you look at the options
mindsetPrinciples.body: Each scenario hinges on one or two constraints: cost, latency, reliability, compliance, financial risk, or developer trust. Find them first, including qualifiers buried in long sentences, then reject every option that breaks them. Several options usually 'work'. Only one satisfies everything the stem says. Candidates who passed (fullstacknrj, Yu, Moanga) all describe this as the core habit.
mindsetPrinciples.example: 'Blocking pre-merge check' means latency matters, so the Message Batches API (up to 24 hours, no SLA) is out even though it is 50% cheaper. The overnight tech-debt report has no such constraint, so batch is right there.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Deterministic controls beat prompt hopes
mindsetPrinciples.body: When an action must always or never happen (verify identity before a refund, block refunds over $500, require clinician review), a prompt instruction is not enough because it has a non-zero failure rate. Use programmatic enforcement such as hooks, prerequisite gates, permission deny rules, schemas or validators. Prompts and few-shot examples are for guidance where an occasional miss is cheap.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Official sample Q1: the agent skips get_customer in 12% of cases. The answer is a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until a verified customer ID exists, not a stronger system prompt or more few-shot examples.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Start with the simplest proportionate fix
mindsetPrinciples.body: The exam rewards the answer that solves the stated problem with the least machinery. Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' says to start simple and add complexity only when it clearly helps. Separate classifiers, routing layers, extra agents and ML infrastructure are over-engineering when a better description, explicit criteria or one structural change fixes the root cause.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Official sample Q3: escalation is miscalibrated. Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples to the system prompt. Don't train a separate classifier (over-engineered) or use sentiment analysis (wrong signal).

mindsetPrinciples.title: Fix the layer where the problem actually lives
mindsetPrinciples.body: Read the evidence in the stem (logs, which component behaved correctly) and fix the component that caused the failure. Don't patch a downstream symptom. Wrong answers often blame components that did exactly what they were told, or reach for the three classic disguises: more examples, a bigger model, or asking the model to check itself.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Official sample Q7: every subagent succeeded, yet reports covered only visual arts. The coordinator split 'creative industries' too narrowly. Professional sample 3: confident wrong answers right after a document refresh point to retrieval and indexing, not the model.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Least privilege: remove what the role doesn't need
mindsetPrinciples.body: Give each agent only the tools its role requires. Too many tools (around 18 instead of 4–5) makes tool selection less reliable, and tools outside an agent's specialty get misused. Removing a capability eliminates the risk. Logging, confirmation prompts and audits are only detective or compensating controls. When a role needs something narrow often, add a narrowly scoped tool rather than the full toolset.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Professional sample 1: support staff only read tickets and draft replies, so remove the refund and delete tools entirely rather than adding logging. Foundations Q9: give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool, not every web search tool.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Tool descriptions are the interface
mindsetPrinciples.body: The model chooses tools mainly from their descriptions. Minimal or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting. The first fix is a description that states what the tool does, its input formats, example queries, edge cases and when to use it instead of a similar tool. Rename or split tools whose purposes overlap. Also check the system prompt for keyword-sensitive wording that pulls the model away from the right tool.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Official sample Q2: get_customer and lookup_order both had one-line descriptions. Expanding the descriptions beats adding 5–8 few-shot examples (token overhead), a routing layer (over-engineered) or merging them into one tool (more effort than a first step warrants).

mindsetPrinciples.title: Context is a budget, so spend it on purpose
mindsetPrinciples.body: Every token in the window competes for the model's attention. Accuracy drops as context grows ('context rot', 'lost in the middle'). Trim verbose tool output to the fields that matter, put key findings at the start, keep exact facts in a persistent block outside summarized history, send verbose exploration to subagents, and load conventions only when they are needed (path rules, skills).
mindsetPrinciples.example: An order lookup returns 40+ fields when 5 matter. Trim it before it piles up. Keep amounts, dates and order IDs in a 'case facts' block, because progressive summarization turns '$247.50 refund on order #8812' into 'a refund was discussed'.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Nothing is inherited, so pass context explicitly
mindsetPrinciples.body: Subagents start with fresh, isolated context. They do not see the coordinator's history or share memory. The prompt you hand them is the only channel. The same applies to human handoffs (the human has no transcript) and to resumed sessions after code changes. Pass complete findings, IDs and metadata in a structured form.
mindsetPrinciples.example: The synthesis subagent needs the web search results and document analysis pasted into its prompt, each with its source URL and date. An escalation to a human needs customer ID, root cause, refund amount and recommended action.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Fail loudly, with structure
mindsetPrinciples.body: Errors should carry enough information for someone to decide what to do next: error category (transient, validation, business, permission), whether a retry makes sense, what was attempted, any partial results and possible alternatives. Never report a failure as an empty success. Never kill the whole workflow over one recoverable failure. Treat a source you couldn't reach differently from a query that legitimately returned nothing.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Official sample Q8: the web search subagent times out. Return structured error context (failure type, query, partial results, alternatives) to the coordinator. Don't return a generic 'search unavailable', an empty result marked as success, or a top-level crash.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Don't let the author grade its own work
mindsetPrinciples.body: A model reviewing its own output in the same session keeps its reasoning and rarely questions its own choices. Use an independent instance with no generator context, split large reviews into focused passes, and check output downstream with validators. Self-reported confidence and 'please double-check' instructions are weak controls.
mindsetPrinciples.example: For CI code review, run a separate Claude instance rather than asking the generating session to review itself. For a 14-file PR, review each file, then run a cross-file integration pass. A bigger context window or majority voting across three runs is the wrong fix.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Calibrate signals; don't trust them blindly
mindsetPrinciples.body: LLM self-reported confidence, customer sentiment and aggregate accuracy are poor proxies on their own. Calibrate confidence thresholds against labeled validation sets, measure accuracy by document type and field, use stratified sampling to find new error patterns, and treat metadata from untrusted servers (MCP annotations) as untrusted.
mindsetPrinciples.example: 97% overall extraction accuracy can hide a 70% failure rate on handwritten invoices. Check each segment before you reduce human review. When a customer lookup returns several matches, ask for another identifier instead of guessing.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Match the mechanism to the workload's profile
mindsetPrinciples.body: Pick the API, model and feature that fit the latency, cost and volume profile. Use synchronous calls when someone is waiting and batch for overnight bulk work. Cache a stable prefix (static content first, changing content last). Use plan mode for architectural or multi-file work and direct execution for well-scoped fixes. Use skills for on-demand procedures and CLAUDE.md for standards that should always apply.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Professional sample 2: an 8,000-token system prompt and policy repeat on every request, so put the static content first and enable prompt caching. A monolith-to-microservices migration calls for plan mode. A one-line date validation calls for direct execution.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Preserve facts, sources and uncertainty end to end
mindsetPrinciples.body: Every hop (summary, subagent, synthesis) can lose attribution or precision. Require structured claim-to-source mappings with dates. Keep conflicting values side by side with their sources rather than picking one. Mark which findings are well supported and which have gaps. Use nullable fields so the model can say 'not present' instead of making something up.
mindsetPrinciples.example: Two credible sources give different market-size figures. The report shows both with source and date, in a 'contested' section. An extraction schema makes 'invoice_due_date' nullable so it isn't invented when the document has none.

mindsetPrinciples.title: Own the system in production (Professional)
mindsetPrinciples.body: At Professional level the architect owns the whole lifecycle: discovery, design, handoff, monitoring and iteration. Governance follows where the data actually flows, not what the contracts say. Human review must be a real gate with clear criteria, not a rubber stamp. Explain trade-offs in business terms (cost, risk, SLA) and agree on success metrics before you build.
mindsetPrinciples.example: A healthcare client needs clinician sign-off before patient replies go out. Build it as a workflow gate the system cannot bypass, log every approval, and agree with stakeholders on the turnaround SLA. Don't just tell the model to 'have a clinician review'.

examDayChecklist: Confirm eligibility early: registration currently needs a Claude Partner Network organization and a company email domain.
Read the official exam guide again the day before, especially the sample questions and their explanations.
Online (OnVUE): install the Pearson proctoring software and run the system test (camera, mic, network, screen recording) a day ahead.
Online: use one monitor only. Disconnect extras, close every other app and tab, and run no AI assistants, translators, IDEs or note apps.
Clear your desk. Phone, smartwatch, headphones and notes must be out of reach, or locked away at a test center.
Bring valid, unexpired, government-issued photo ID whose name matches your registration exactly (Latin script).
Check in 30 minutes early. Check-in and room scans take time.
Expect to accept an NDA at the start. Declining ends the session with no refund.
Pace yourself at under 2 minutes per question (60 items or 63 items in 120 minutes). Answer every item on the first pass and flag the hard ones.
Each multiple-response item tells you how many answers to pick. Select exactly that many.
For each question, find the constraint and the qualifiers first, strike out clearly wrong options, then choose the simplest option that fixes the root cause.
With the time left, go through flagged items on the Review screen. Change an answer only for a concrete reason.
Online: stay connected after you finish until the session recording has uploaded.
Results can take from a few days to about 2 weeks. If you need a retake, the waits are 14, 30 and 90 days, and each attempt is paid.
commonMistakes: Relying on system-prompt instructions or few-shot examples when the requirement needs a guarantee. Use hooks, prerequisite gates, schemas or permission rules.
Picking the most sophisticated architecture (extra agents, classifiers, routing layers) when a simpler fix meets every requirement.
Falling for the three disguises: add more examples, switch to a bigger model, or ask the model to check itself.
Assuming subagents inherit the coordinator's conversation or share memory. Context has to be passed in the Task prompt.
Ending the agent loop by parsing assistant text or using an iteration cap as the main stop condition, instead of checking stop_reason ('tool_use' to continue, 'end_turn' to stop).
Treating stop_reason 'max_tokens' as success. The output was cut off.
Returning empty results marked as success when a tool times out, or returning a generic 'operation failed' that hides the error category and whether a retry makes sense.
Escalating on negative sentiment or low self-reported confidence instead of explicit criteria (customer asks for a human, a policy gap, or no progress).
Investigating first when the customer has explicitly asked for a human. Honor that request immediately.
Choosing a customer from several matches by heuristic instead of asking for another identifier.
Putting shared team commands or instructions in ~/.claude/... (personal) instead of the project's .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, CLAUDE.md or .mcp.json.
Using a per-directory CLAUDE.md for conventions that apply to scattered files (such as tests). Use .claude/rules/ with a paths glob like **/*.test.tsx.
Using plan mode for trivial single-file fixes, or skipping it for architectural, multi-file migrations.
Running Claude Code in CI without -p, or inventing flags such as --batch or CLAUDE_HEADLESS.
Thinking tool_use or JSON schemas guarantee correct content. They prevent syntax errors, but values can still be wrong, so validate meaning downstream.
Making every schema field required, which pushes the model to invent values. Make fields nullable when the source may not contain them.
Retrying an extraction when the information isn't in the source document. A retry can't fix missing data.
Sending blocking or latency-sensitive work (pre-merge checks) to the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours with no SLA and no multi-turn tool calls.
Giving one agent every tool. More tools make selection less reliable, and out-of-role tools get misused.
Adding logging or confirmation prompts when least privilege calls for removing the capability.
Believing a bigger context window fixes inconsistent reviews of many files. That is attention dilution, so split the work into per-file passes plus an integration pass.
Summarizing away exact amounts, dates and IDs instead of keeping them in a persistent case-facts block.
Choosing one of two conflicting sources arbitrarily instead of showing both with attribution and dates.
Professional: putting volatile content before the stable prefix, which breaks prompt caching.
Professional: blaming the model for confident wrong answers right after a data refresh. Check retrieval and indexing first.
Memorizing practice-exam answers. Real questions are reworded and longer, and practice scores tend to overstate readiness.
